blogs.title: Procedural Rights in Vacuo: AFL v. Greer and the Limits of Procedural Standing
blogs.description: This post examines the D.C. Circuit's application of the 'procedural right in vacuo' doctrine from Summers v. Earth Island Institute, explaining how the court held that AFL's asserted statutory right to an OSC investigation under § 1216 could not, without a concrete affected interest, supply Article III standing on its own. The post situates this ruling within the broader trajectory of the D.C. Circuit's procedural standing jurisprudence—including Citizens for Constitutional Integrity v. Census Bureau and Center for Law & Education v. Department of Education—to analyze how courts distinguish between procedural rights that are tethered to concrete interests and those that are asserted in the abstract. It also explores the court's choice not to decide whether AFL's alleged injuries were procedural or substantive, given that AFL failed even the relaxed standing requirements for procedural injuries, and considers the implications for future plaintiffs seeking to compel agency oversight.

blogs.title: The Speculative Chain: Redressability and Multi-Agency Causation in Standing Analysis
blogs.description: This post focuses on the D.C. Circuit's redressability and causation analysis, which rejected AFL's theory that an OSC investigation would ultimately lead DOJ to produce the requested FOIA records. The court found the causal chain—running from OSC investigation, to possible MSPB sanctions, to possible DOJ compliance—too speculative under FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine and Haaland v. Brackeen. The post analyzes how this ruling fits into a broader pattern of courts rejecting standing theories that depend on the independent choices of non-party actors, and specifically examines the court's invocation of Heckler v. Chaney's enforcement discretion principle within a standing analysis—a notable doctrinal move that imports a merits-based concept into the jurisdictional inquiry. The post considers whether this conflation of enforcement discretion with redressability is analytically sound and what it signals for future attempts to compel oversight agencies to act.

blogs.title: Informational Standing Without an Entitlement: What AFL v. Greer Tells Us About the Boundaries of Informational Injury
blogs.description: This post analyzes the court's rejection of AFL's second standing theory—its claim that it suffered an informational injury by being denied the fruits of an OSC investigation. The court drew a critical distinction between statutes that entitle plaintiffs to receive information (such as those at issue in FEC v. Akins and Public Citizen v. DOJ) and § 1216, which may require an investigation but creates no entitlement for the complainant to receive information. The post examines the significance of this distinction for informational standing doctrine, particularly in light of AFL's argument that § 1214's notice requirements could be engrafted onto § 1216 investigations. The post explores the broader question of when a statutory mandate to investigate or act translates into an individual entitlement to information sufficient to confer standing, and what this means for requesters seeking to use oversight mechanisms as alternative FOIA enforcement tools.

blogs.title: The Merits Question Left Unanswered: § 1216, § 552(a)(4)(F)(i), and the Architecture of FOIA Oversight
blogs.description: This post examines the significant statutory interpretation question the D.C. Circuit never reached: whether FOIA's own enforcement provision in § 552(a)(4)(F)(i)—with its three predicates for triggering an OSC investigation—limits OSC's independent authority to investigate arbitrary FOIA withholdings under § 1216 of the Civil Service Reform Act. The district court held that § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) does not constrain § 1216's broader investigative mandate, a ruling that remains on the books despite the D.C. Circuit's disposition. The post analyzes the textual and structural arguments for and against treating these provisions as independent or interlocking, considers how the Sixth Circuit's Carson v. OSC decision fits into the picture, and discusses the practical implications of the district court's reading for the future of FOIA oversight. It also reflects on the broader institutional question of whether courts should reach statutory interpretation questions when standing defects could leave agency oversight authority in a state of unresolved uncertainty.
